t: The hill was first fortified in 1333, and the castle seen today was largely built by Ikeda Terumasa between 1601 and 1609, a work believed to have taken 2.5 million man-days of labour.
Its gates, baileys and walls were laid out so that an approaching force would travel in a spiral, but the castle was never attacked in this manner and the system remains untested.

It was spared demolition in the Meiji Period, survived the bombing of Himeji in 1945 and the Great Hanshin earthquake of 1995, and was registered in 1993 as one of the first World Heritage Sites in Japan.
dyk: The straight distance from the Hishi Gate to the main keep is only 130 metres, but the path between them is 325 metres long.
ev: Akamatsu Norimura fortified Himeyama hill during the Genkō War
His son Sadanori demolished the fort and built Himeyama Castle in its place
Toyotomi Hideyoshi expanded the castle and built a three-storey keep
Ikeda Terumasa began to rebuild the castle completely, work that lasted until 1609
Honda Tadamasa inherited the castle and added several buildings, including the Dressing Tower for Princess Sen
The castle was abandoned and the whole complex was slated for demolition, but Nakamura Shigeto spared it
Himeji was heavily bombed, and the castle survived intact
The castle was registered as one of the first World Heritage Sites in Japan

f.made: Fortified by Akamatsu Norimura in 1333, remodelled by the Kuroda clan and by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, rebuilt by Ikeda Terumasa from 1601 to 1609 and extended by Honda Tadamasa from 1617 to 1618
f.form: A hirayama (flat hilltop) castle of stone and wood with white plaster walls: a main keep 46.4 metres high with three smaller keeps, 83 buildings, three moats and a spiral approach, on a complex of 233 hectares
f.where: On the hill called Himeyama, 45.6 metres above sea level, in the centre of Himeji, Hyōgo Prefecture, Japan
f.known: the white plaster exterior that gave it the names Hakuro-jō and Shirasagi-jō; the maze of paths to the keep; roughly 1,000 loopholes; five National Treasures; survival of the 1945 bombing and the 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake; registration as a World Heritage Site in 1993
